Abstract: Electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO2) conversion is promising to balance the carbon cycle for
human society. However, efficient electrocatalyst is the key to determine the selective conversion of CO2
toward valuable products. We report herein an efficient La2CuO4 perovskite catalyst for electrochemical CO2 reduction. A high Faradaic efficiency of 56.3% with a partial current density of 117 mA cm-2 is achieved for
methane production over this perovskite catalyst at -1.4 V (vs. RHE). Results demonstrate that the structural
evolution of La2CuO4 perovskite take place simultaneously during the cathodic CO2 reduction process.
Theoretical investigations further unravel that the emerged Cu/La2CuO4 interface accounts for the CO2
methanation behaviors. This work provides an effective perovskite electrocatalyst for the ambient CO2
methanation and offers valuable understandings in the structure evolution and surface reconstruction of pre-
catalysts in the catalytic reactions for energy-relevant technologies.
Keyword: Carbon dioxide reduction; Electrocatalyst; Perovskite; Methane; Structure evolution.

The dramatic increase in carbon dioxide (CO2) emission has a severe consequence on the global climate, leading to massive threats to mankind.1 Chemical conversion of CO2 into valuable products is more desirable for reducing the accumulation of CO2 and maintaining carbon cycle.2-3 Compared with the traditional thermal
conversion at high temperature, electrochemical CO2 conversion driven by the sustainable power sources is more promising due to its mild operation conditions.4-5 However, multiple products are often generated during
the complex proton-coupled-electron multistep of CO2 reduction because of the inevitable competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and diverging reactions.6-7 Therefore, high-efficiency electrocatalyst is of
prime significance for selective CO2 reduction.8-10 Among various popular catalysts, copper (Cu) compounds,
especially oxides-derived Cu catalysts, demonstrate the advantages in producing hydrocarbons from the CO2 reduction.11-12 However, these oxides are still limited at high selectivity for the specific hydrocarbons, for
example, methane (CH4), which is desired for subsequent chemical fuels and industrial process.13 Moreover,
these oxide-derived Cu catalysts often suffer from the structural evolution and surface reconstruction during
the cathodic CO2 reduction.14-16 Therefore, developing efficient Cu-based catalyst for producing hydrocarbon
and understanding the working mechanism are crucial and yet challenging.
Recently, perovskite materials entice considerable courtesy in the photoelectric technologies.17 Perovskite
oxides have the flexible electronic structure with a general chemical formula of ABO3,18 where A is rare earth,
alkaline metal or other ions with a large radius, and B represents transition metal. In which, the A sites hold
the structure, and the B sites would account for the catalytic activity.19 With this unique structure, perovskites
exhibit diverse physical and chemical properties, such as the electromagnetic property and catalytic activity
for CO2 reduction.20-22 For instance, a perovskite oxide of La0.6Sr0.4Fe0.8Ni0.2O3-δ demonstrated an efficient conversion of CO2 to carbon monoxide (CO) in a high-temperature solid oxide electrolysis cell.23 The in-situ
exsolved Fe-Ni bimetallic alloy uniformly socked on an oxygen-deficient perovskite, which contributed to the

CO generation. Another example is a redox-stable perovskite of Ni/Cu co-doped La0.75Sr0.25Cr0.5Mn0.5O3-d, which was employed in converting CO2 to CO at a high temperature.24 However, these perovskite oxides are
highlighted as the advanced materials in the solid oxide electrolysis cells for the electrochemical CO2 activation and conversion at high temperature,25-26 few reports demonstrate for the ambient CO2 electroreduction.27 Moreover, these reduction systems employed by perovskite oxide catalysts often
demonstrate the CO generation, while the value-added hydrocarbons such as CH4 are seldom reported.28-29
Herein, we report a perovskite oxide of La2CuO4 as the efficient catalyst for the electrochemically ambient
conversion of CO2 toward CH4 generation. La2CuO4 is a kind of K2NiF4 type structure, which is formed by stacking CuO2 layer and the rock salt LaO layer (Figure 1a).30-31 Each Cu atom is surrounded by six oxygen
atoms, the formed CuO6 octahedral coordination leads to apex angle interconnected octahedron perovskite
CuO2 layer, where two LaO layers separate the CuO2 layer. The unique electronic configuration of La2CuO4
perovskite is supposed to provide abundant active sites for CO2 electrocatalysis. Considerably, a high Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 56.3% with a partial current density of 117 mA cm-2 for CH4 is achieved over this La2CuO4
perovskite catalyst at -1.4 V vs. RHE. Experimental results and theoretical analysis show that the Cu species
are partially exsolved from the perovskite and reduced to the metallic Cu on the perovskite surface, and the
resultant Cu/La2CuO4 heterostructure might be responsible for the efficient CO2 methanation process. This
work offers an effective perovskite catalyst for selective electrochemical CO2 conversion and may provide
valuable understandings in the structural evolution and surface reconstruction of pre-catalysts for
electrochemical reactions and beyond.
The crystalline La2CuO4 perovskite is obtained by a sol-gel method followed by the calcination at 800 °C
for 10 h. Powder x-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern shows the well-identified peaks at 24.3°, 31.1°, and 33.4°,
47.8° (Figure 1b), corresponding to the (111), (113) and (200), (220) planes of the orthorhombic La2CuO4

(PDF: 38-0709), respectively. Moreover, no characteristic peaks corresponding to La2O3, Cu2O, and CuO are
observed, suggesting the pure phase of La2CuO4 perovskite. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image
presents the morphological structure of perovskite oxide. The interconnected network is composed of particles
with the size of ~300-500 nm, leaving a highly porous layered fragment (Figure 1c). High-resolution
transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image reveals the d-spacing of 0.37 nm, which is corresponding
to the (111) plane of perovskite La2CuO4 crystal (Figure 1d). The corresponding selected-area electron
diffraction (SAED) pattern shows the bright diffraction dots (Figure 1d inset), suggesting the single-crystal
nature of the as-prepared La2CuO4 perovskite. Furthermore, the elemental mapping patterns exhibit the
uniform distribution of La, Cu, and O elements (Figure 1e). The corresponding element ratio of La and Cu
measured by electron dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) is 1.98: 1, which is close to the standard
stoichiometric ratio of La2CuO4 perovskite (Figure S1).
The CO2 reduction of the as-fabricated La2CuO4 is firstly recorded in 0.1 M KHCO3 in an H-type cell
(Figure S2). Compared with the Ar-saturated electrolyte, a significant response of current density is observed
in the CO2-saturated electrolyte, which suggests a possible CO2 reduction activity (Figure S3a). Moreover, a
small cathodic peak at -1.0 V would be ascribed to the partial reduction of Cu species in the La2CuO4
perovskite. To further understand the product distribution and analyze the reaction selectivity, the
chronoamperometric electrolysis measurements (Figure S3b) are monitored by online gas chromatography
(GC) for gas products and offline nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy for liquid products
(Figure S4). Among the total FE of ~85% for gaseous products, a maximum FE of 62% with a partial current
density of 4.2 mA cm-2 for CH4 is stably achieved at -1.3 V vs. RHE (Figure S3c, 3d). The gas diffusion
electrodes for CO2 reduction are then prepared and measured in the home-made flow cell configurations
(Figure S5). The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves are recorded in 1.0 M KOH purged with CO2.

Compared with the H-cell results, a much higher current density of 205 mA cm-2 is achieved at -1.4 V vs.
RHE in the CO2 reduction environment (Figure 2a). Such a significant enhancement of current density in the
flow cell is mainly ascribed to the improved CO2 concentration in the gas diffusion electrode and reduced
solution resistance in the flow cell (Figure S6). Moreover, the step electrolysis also shows the corresponding
improved current density at each potential (Figure 2b). At -1.4 V vs. RHE, the current density reaches ~208
mA cm-2, which is similar to the LSV record. The product distribution is also monitored by the online GC and
NMR systems (Figure S7). Among all products, the FE of the dominant CH4 increases along with the
increased potential (Figure 2c). Moreover, the small FE of H2 (<20%) also indicates a well-inhibited HER
over the all-potential range. Specifically, the FE of ~56.3% for CH4 is achieved at -1.4 V vs. RHE, which is close to the H-cell results (Figure 2c). And the partial current density of CH4 is 117 mA cm-2, which is almost
28 times than that in H-cell. Compared with CuO catalyst obtained by the similar method (Figure S8), a much
lower FE (~20%) and smaller partial current density (1.0 mA cm-2 in H-cell and 30.0 mA cm-2 in flow cell)
for CH4 are afforded at the same potential (Figure S9). Besides, the La2CuO4 perovskite treated by hydrogen
reduction (named H-La2CuO4) is also performed, which contains the mixture of separated Cu and La2O3 (Figure S10). The CH4 FEs of 23% and 11% with smaller current densities of 3.0 and 210.0 mA cm-2 are
achieved in the H-cell and flow cell configurations, respectively (Figure S11). All the above results suggest
the La2CuO4 perovskite is better than CuO and H-La2CuO4 for the CO2 conversion to CH4. Furthermore, the
chronoamperometry test in Figure 2d also verifies the continuous and stable CO2 reduction toward CH4
production. Compared with other reported catalysts for CO2 reduction, the La2CuO4 perovskite displays a
considerable FE and the highest CH4 partial current density (Table S1), suggesting the promising potential of
perovskite catalyst for the electrochemical CO2 conversion.

As the La2CuO4 perovskite oxide would suffer the reduction or exsolution during the cathodic CO2
electrolysis, a series of characterizations are performed on the cathodized La2CuO4 perovskite to investigate
the structural evolution. After the 1000 s electrolysis, XRD pattern of the cathodized perovskite indicates the
preserved La2CuO4 phase (Figure 3a, S12), while a new peak appeared at ~43.3° is attributed to the emergence
of metallic Cu (PDF 04-0836). SEM observations show the surface of perovskite oxide becomes rougher after
the electrolysis, even the whole particle morphology is still remained (Figure S13). There are some small
particles exsolved from the perovskite substrate (Figure 3b), which would be indexed as the Cu clusters on
the cathodized La2CuO4. HRTEM image verifies the presence of Cu clusters on the substrate and the formation
of Cu/La2CuO4 heterostructure (Figure 3c). The inter-planar spaces with 0.37 and 0.21 nm correspond to the
La2CuO4(111) and Cu(111), respectively. Moreover, the SAED pattern demonstrates the preservation of
single-crystal La2CuO4 and the emergence of polycrystalline Cu in the cathodized La2CuO4 perovskite (Figure
3c inset). In addition to the morphological changes, the elemental distribution is also changed after the
electrochemical process (Figure 3d). EDS elemental mapping shows the uniform distribution of La and O
elements. However, some Cu aggregations are observed accompanying with the uniform distribution of La
and O in the substrate (Figure 3d). The interface of the La2CuO4 substrate and evolved Cu species could be
found in the cathodized La2CuO4 (Figure S13c). Besides, the slightly increased atomic ratio (1.32: 1) of La
and Cu also suggest the partial segregation of Cu on the substrate surface (Figure S13d). The above results
indicate the near surface Cu species at B sites of La2CuO4 perovskite would be partially reduced during the
cathodic CO2 reduction process. It can be explained by the high mobility of Cu in the La2CuO4 perovskite,
which would lead to the dissolution and redeposition of Cu ions at the large overpotentials and current
densities during the cathodic CO2 reduction process.32 Similar phenomena is happened in the CuO catalysts,
the metallic Cu clusters are also found on the substrate particles after the CO2 electrolysis (Figure S8). While

The structural evolution and reconstruction would determine the electronic structure of Cu/La2CuO4
composite. The chemical composition and valence state of the perovskite oxides before and after the
electrolysis are then investigated by x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) technique (Figure S14a). The
binding energy of La 3d is almost same before and after the electrolysis, indicating La ions would not be
involved in the redox process (Figure S14b). In the initial La2CuO4 perovskite, the binding energy of 932.7 eV is corresponding to Cu 2p3/2 (Figure 4a).33 After the electrolysis, the Cu 2p3/2 signal is deconvoluted into two peaks, the peak at 931.6 eV is referred to Cu(0),34 and another peak at 933.3 eV corresponds to Cu(II) for
La2CuO4. The negative shift of Cu 2p and emergence of Cu(0) suggest that the electrons are more natural to transfer at the interface of Cu/La2CuO4.35-37 Moreover, the satellite spectra of the cathodized La2CuO4 are
flatter compared with the initial counterpart, which also evidence the reduced Cu valance state. Furthermore,
the peaks of O 1s for initial La2CuO4 located at 528.4 and 531.1 eV are assigned to the surface lattice oxygen
species (perovskite lattice termination) and adsorbed oxygen or hydroxyl (−OH/O2), respectively (Figure 4b).38 However, the O 1s profile of the cathodized La2CuO4 displays a different shape, the new peaks at 527.9 eV and 529.8 eV would be referred to Cu−O and O22-/O−.39 All the above results suggest the evolution of
La2CuO4 perovskite and formation of metallic Cu species in the Cu/La2CuO4 heterostructure. This process
would optimize the surface adsorption of CO2 and charge transfer, then the compatible heterostructure interface are vital to promote the electrochemical CO2 reduction.40-42 As shown in Figure 4c, the cathodized
La2CuO4 shows a higher CO2 adsorption capacity than the initial La2CuO4. Moreover, the electrochemical
impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is performed to discuss the charge transfer capability (Figure 4d). The
semicircle diameter of the Nyquist plot for the cathodized La2CuO4 (Rct=9.6 Ω) is much smaller than that of

Compared with the H-La2CuO4 and CuO samples, the cathodized La2CuO4 is also more favorable in the charge
transfer, implying the advantages of in-situ formed Cu/La2CuO4 heterostructure (Figure S6). These ex-situ
results suggest the Cu/La2CuO4 interfaces may account for the efficient CO2 reduction. In order to further
study the structure evolution, the in-situ Raman characterizations are conducted in the H-cell system. The in-
situ Raman spectra indicate that the La2CuO4 catalyst suffers from the surface evolution during the
electrochemical CO2 reduction (Figure S15). Without the cathode potential applied, the initial La2CuO4 displays five Raman peaks at 695, 904, 1165, 1214 and 1412 cm-1, referring to the typical perovskite structure.
After applying -1.4 V for 0.5 h, the typical peaks of La2CuO4 are remained without obvious change. Further
increasing the reduction time, the intensity of Raman peaks shows some slight decrease, indicating the surface
structure evolution and reconstruction of La2CuO4. Besides, the Raman peaks basically stay unchanged after
3 h, suggesting the equilibrium of the (sub)surface reconstruction on the formed Cu/La2CuO4 composite.
Based on the previous results, a possible mechanistic model is proposed for the electrochemical CO2 methanation (Figure 5).43-44 During the cathodic CO2 reduction, Cu at the near surface of La2CuO4 is the
partially reduced and formed an optimized Cu/La2CuO4 heterostructure (Figure 5a), which endows the synergistic effect of endorsing CO2 adsorption and charge transfer interfaces.45-47 The formation energy of
surface oxygen vacancy (VO) of La2CuO4(111) is 1.26 eV, and accordingly, the surface oxygen of
La2CuO4(111) is easily removed (Figure S16). In the parent La2CuO4, Cu atoms in the CuO6 octahedrons
would be partially reduced under the cathodic process accompanied by the coordination change of the Cu ions
at B sites. With the spillover of Cu atoms, the metallic Cu phase is formed as well as La2O3, and the d-band
center of the Cu atoms is down-shifted (Figure S17). The Bader charges of Cu atoms on La2CuO4(111) and
in the parent La2CuO4 bulk are +0.68 and 0.88 e, respectively (Table S2). Notably, Bader charges of Cu atoms

have a good linear dependence on the position of their d-band center (Figure S18). The Bader charge of the
interfacial Cu atoms in Cu/La2CuO4 is +0.16 e, indicating a low-degree oxidation due to the strong metalsupport interactions (MSI).48-50 Comparing with the initial La2CuO4, the positive shift of Cu XPS peaks for
Cu/La2CuO4 suggests the Cu species exposed at the outer surface of La2CuO4 are partially oxidized. The
interfacial Cu atoms can improve the CO2 adsorption and activation. As shown in Figure 5b, the determined
potential energy profile of CO2 methanation is analyzed by the density functional theory (DFT) simulations.
The CO2 adsorption energy on the Cu(111) and La2CuO4(111) facets is negligible (Figure S16), while it is
improved by 0.31 eV over the interface of Cu/La2CuO4. Besides, the interface of Cu/La2CuO4 generally
provides a stronger adsorption of HxCO (x = 1~3) intermediates than Cu(111) (Figure S19). The overpotential
of CO2 methanation over Cu(111) and Cu/La2CuO4 is 0.92 and 0.70 eV, respectively (Table S3). Therefore,
the MSI synergistically adjusts the electronic structures of Cu/La2CuO4, and as a result improves its electro-
catalytic activity for the CO2 methanation.
In summary, a La2CuO4 perovskite catalyst is reported for the selective electrochemical CO2 reduction toward CH4 production. A high FE of 56.3% with a partial current density of 117 mA cm-2 for CH4 is achieved
over this cathodized perovskite catalyst at -1.4 V vs. RHE. Results and analysis demonstrate that the structural
evolution of La2CuO4 perovskite and formation of Cu/La2CuO4 heterostructure are happened simultaneously
during the cathodic CO2 methanation. Theoretical investigations further confirm that the interfacial Cu atoms
of Cu/La2CuO4 would be responsible for the admirable activity of CO2 methanation. This work provides an
effective perovskite electrocatalyst for ambient electrochemical CO2 methanation and may offer valuable
understandings in the structure evolution and surface reconstruction of electrocatalytic materials during the
electrochemical reactions in energy-relevant technologies.
